messages.subject: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: follow up
parts:
Dear all,

thanks to your help (and to data augmentation) I have managed to code a running (and converging) Poisson model for the effect of 4 experimental treatments on the size of 12 freshwater snail populations in 12 separated ponds (code pasted below). I have mainly used Royle, Converse and Link 2012 (arXiv), which provide two codes for that type of experimental design. However, I still have some major issues:

1) I don't really know how to deal with the two ponds (#1 and #7) in which no snail was observed (i.e., all intially introduced snails died, which is obviously a strong indication of an experimental effect). For now I use one single 00 capture history for each of these snail-absent ponds. Increasing number of 00 observations (to 20 and 100, obs object in the code) does not affect estimates of total N (the sum of all population sizes) or capture probability p, but strongly homogenizes group membership probabilities (such that estimated pop sizes become quite similar among ponds). Also, DIC increases.

2) I have a complete lack of fit (bayesian p-value of 0, very large ratio of Eobs and Esim). I have tried the negative binomial version of the model in Royle, Converse and Link 2012 (see second code pasted below) but get all negative estimates. Before really trying to understand this silly result I would like to increase the fit of the Poisson model, but don't really see how to do it.

3) To help increasing model fit I tried to make detection probability p treatment- or population- specific but, again, did not manage to do it.

Hopefully somme of you could help me with that...

Many thanks!

éric


#### DATA
bac <- c(1:12)                            #pop indices
trait <- c(rep(c("C","S","P","SP"), 3))                #experimental treatments
n <-c(0, 20, 19, 7, 1, 20, 0, 135, 30, 190, 14, 17)        #nb captured and marked at occasion 1
recapt <-  c(0, 21, 18, 8, 1, 23, 0, 150, 42, 251, 18, 28)    #nb recaptured
mk <- c(0, 20, 17, 7, 1, 20 , 0, 134, 30, 186, 14, 17)        #nb marked among recaptures at occasion 2
un <- (recapt - mk)                        #nb unmarked among recaptures at occasion 2
tobs <- n + (un)                        #total number of observed individuals
#### BUILD AUGMENTATED DATASET
#Data alone, generate 1 line with 0s for populations in which no snail was observed (pops 1 and 7)
obs <- 100    #number of lines for populations in which no individual was observed
data <- NULL
for(i in 1:length(bac)){
    if (i == 1 | i == 7) {nb <- obs} else {nb <- n[i] + un[i]}    #total number of different individuals observed
    pop <- rep(bac[i], times = nb)
    treat <- rep(trait[i], times = nb)
    y <- if (i == 1 | i == 7) rep(0, nb) else c(rep(2, times = mk[i]), rep(1, times = nb - mk[i]))
    data <- rbind(data, data.frame(pop, treat, y))
}

#Data augmentation
M <- 2000    #final size of the augmented dataset
A <- M - dim(data)[1]    #number of added individuals to reach of total pop size of M
data <- rbind(data, data.frame(pop = rep(NA, A), treat = rep(NA, A), y = rep(0, A)))

#### POISSON MODEL SPECIFICATION
setwd("~/Documents/Limnees/Article_Loïc")
cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen_poisson.jags", "
model{
### priors and constraints
  p ~ dunif(0, 1)
  for(j in 1:tr){
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.1)
    }
  psi <- sum(lam[])/M

  for(i in 1:M){
    g[i] ~ dcat(gprobs[])
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    y[i] ~ dbin(mu[i], K)
   mu[i] <- z[i]*p
    }

### likelihood
# abundance model
  for(s in 1:S){
    gprobs[s] <- lam[s]/sum(lam[1:S])
    log(lam[s]) <- beta[treat[s]]
    #goodness of fit
    Eobs[s] <- pow(tobs[s] - sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s])    #Xobs in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
    Esim[s] <- pow(lam[s]*p - sum(lam[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(lam[])*gprobs[s])     #Xsim in Royle, Converse & Link 2012 
  }
#### derived quantities
N <- sum(z[1:M])
fit <- sum(Eobs[])
fit.new <- sum(Esim[])
}
")

## 2) Data list
jags.data <- list(y = data$y, g = data$pop, tr = length(levels(as.factor(trait))), treat = as.numeric(as.factor(trait)), S = length(bac), M = M, K = 2, tobs = tobs)

## 3) Initial values
nhat <- c(0,21,20,8,1,23,0,151,42,256,18,28)    #Chapman ML estimates of pop sizes (from file Pop.number.r)
inits <- function(){list(beta = rep(runif(1, -5, 5), 4), z = rep(1,M), mu.p = runif(1, -1, 1), sd.p = runif(1, 0, 3))}

## 4) Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("lam", "p", "psi", "beta", "N", "fit", "fit.new")

## 5) MCMC settings
ni <- 2000
nt <- 5
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3

#model
library(jagsUI)
mod <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "Lincoln_petersen_poisson.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.adapt = 2000, parallel = TRUE) #DIC 4451




#### NEGATIVE-BINOMIAL MODEL SPECIFICATION
setwd("~/Documents/Limnees/Article_Loïc")
cat(file = "Lincoln_petersen_negbin.jags", "
model{
### priors and constraints
  p ~ dunif(0, 1)
  for(j in 1:tr){
    beta[j] ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)
    }
  a ~ dunif(0, 1000)
  b <- 1
  psi ~ dunif(0,1)

  for(i in 1:M){
    g[i] ~ dcat(gprobs[])
    z[i] ~ dbern(psi)
    y[i] ~ dbin(mu[i], K)
    mu[i] <- z[i]*p
    }
### likelihood
# abundance model
  for(s in 1:S){
    eta[s] ~ dgamma(a,b)
    lam[s] <- beta[treat[s]]
    alpha[s] <- eta[s]*lam[s]
    gprobs[s] <- alpha[s]/sum(alpha[1:S])
    #goodness of fit
    Eobs[s] <- pow(tobs[s] - sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(tobs[])*gprobs[s]) #Xobs in Royle, Converse & Link 2012
    Esim[s] <- pow(lam[s]*p - sum(lam[])*gprobs[s], 2) / (sum(lam[])*gprobs[s]) #Xsim in Royle, Converse & Link 2012  
  }
#### derived quantities
N <- sum(z[1:M])
fit <- sum(Eobs[])
fit.new <- sum(Esim[])
}
")

## 2) Data list
jags.data <- list(y = data$y, g = data$pop, tr = length(levels(as.factor(trait))), treat = as.numeric(as.factor(trait)), S = length(bac), M = M, K = 2, tobs = tobs)

## 3) Initial values
nhat <- c(0,21,20,8,1,23,0,151,42,256,18,28)    #Chapman ML estimates of pop sizes (from file Pop.number.r)
inits <- function(){list(beta = rep(runif(1, -5, 5), 4), z = rep(1,M), p = 0.9)}

## 4) Parameters monitored
parameters <- c("lam", "p", "psi", "beta", "N", "fit", "fit.new")

## 5) MCMC settings
ni <- 2000
nt <- 5
nb <- 1000
nc <- 3

#model
library(jagsUI)
mod <- jags(jags.data, inits, parameters, "Lincoln_petersen_negbin.jags", n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, n.burnin = nb, n.adapt = 2000, parallel = TRUE) #DIC 3876.799

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical Lincoln-Petersen model: follow up
parts:
Eric,

So you failed to collect snails at all during the capture or recapture sessions in ponds 1 and 7?  If you want to include these ponds, a zero-inflated distribution might provide better fit if p is constant.  My guess is that the expected value of N is sufficiently large that the probability of having population = 0 snails in any pond is almost impossible under Poisson or NB distributions (hence the expected values are uniformly larger than the observed?).  Also, I would not fit a model with a factorial, site-specific p: again, there's no information in the data to allow estimation of the parameter for those ponds with no encounters.  Maybe a treatment-specific p would work. 

Actually, scratch that last sentence: I think an additional problem is that the replication is 3 at each treatment level, and it is almost impossible to find an appropriate distribution for lambda or p given that level of replication.  For example, treatment 1 (if I'm reading this correctly) has one pond with no detections whatsoever ,1 pond where 1 snail was encountered twice, and one pond where 30 animals were observed 11, and 12 animals 01.  So in one pond, the expected value of p (if these were treated independently) is 0, in the next it is 1, and in the final it is...uh, I dunno, 0.8 or something?  That's a tough to fit to a distribution.  Similarly, the expected values of N at those sites would be ~infinity, 1, and 50 or something.  Tough to find a good parametric fit there, either.    Yeah, in general, it looks like p is extremely high, but you have a couple of sites with very few--if any--snails.  I think a ZIP or ZINB is the way to go, and maybe the zero inflation parameter is best modeled as a function of treatment as well.


John
